item.title: Bayesian Inference as a Frequentist
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
“As a frequentist, I cannot think of a better statistical tool than the Bayesian posterior.”

— Bas Kleijn, The Frequentist Theory of Bayesian Statistics [1]

Bayesian and frequentist statistics are usually introduced as competing frameworks with key differences. “Probability of an event” can mean something very different to a frequentist than to a bayesian. Frequentists generally consider that data is generated by some true unknown probability distribution, the “data generating process” (DGP) or “true (statistical) model”. Some Bayesians share this belief, but others reject this idea. (Nuances and an extensive discussion is in section 5 in [2].)

How is it then possible that frequentists can use bayesian techniques? Frequentists define estimators and confidence sets as functions of the sample. Points from the posterior (i.e. the posterior mean) are functions of the sample. (Precise definitions are in section 1+2 in [1].) For example, Bradley Efron reinterprets the posterior mean as frequentist point estimator in [3]:

“… regardless of its Bayesian provenance, we consider the (posterior mean) simply as a function of the data x, and compute its frequentist variability.”

The interesting question for the frequentist is what properties this approach has. For example, if you redefine the posterior mean as frequentist point estimator, what is the bias, in the sense of ? In most cases bias can be expected. What about coverage? Depends.

Both questions can be answered with Monte Carlo simulations (MCSs) for selected DGPs: create a list of DGPs assumed to be true and evaluate the desired frequentist properties (i.e. bias, coverage, …) of your approach. (More details on that in [4].)

Many frequentist inferential procedures are often only approximately justified (i.e. based on large sample approximations). MCSs are used to evaluate their properties. If you are a frequentist, you probably have intentionally used biased estimators and evaluated the properties of your inference with MCS. So you may consider bayesian techniques for certain tasks as well.

An interesting + challenging (and likely very emotional!) topic is how to treat & call this grey area / fusion / hybrid approach of bayesian and frequentist statistics.

  • There are bayesian approaches that are designed with frequentist properties in mind.
  • There are (quite old) frequentist approaches that incorporate prior information [5].
  • For many tasks some bayesian & frequentist solutions produce the same numerical output.
  • Key differences in interpreting probability and the view of the existence of a true statistical model remain (i.e. see [2] for an overview).

Like other areas of science, statistics is difficult and not intuitive.

References

[1] Kleijn, B. (2022). The Frequentist Theory of Bayesian Statistics. PDF

[2] Gelman, A. & Hennig, C. (2017). Beyond Subjective and Objective in Statistics. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A. JSTOR

[3] Efron, B. (2015). Frequentist Accuracy of Bayesian Estimates. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B. JSTOR

[4] Kelter, R. (2023). Estimating the Sampling Distribution of Test-Statistics in Bayesian Clinical Trials. arXiv:2306.09151

[5] Theil, H. & Goldberger, A. An Interpretation and Implementation of the Theil-Goldberger ‘Mixed’ Estimator. RePEc

item.title: Wasserman on Bayesian Inference
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
“Bayesian inference is a controversial approach because it inherently embraces a subjective notion of probability. In general, Bayesian methods provide no guarantees on long run performance.”

— Larry Wasserman, All of Statistics [1], chapter 11.

Larry Wasserman is one of the most accomplished theoretical statisticians on the planet. Wasserman definitely knows the theory behind bayesian statistics well: he has extensively published about bayesian statistics in top journals. (You can check his publication list here: https://lnkd.in/e2VrT3Kb)

Here is a quote of Bas Kleijn, who also published extensively about bayesian statistics in top statistical journals:

“As a frequentist, I cannot think of a better statistical tool than the Bayesian posterior.”

— Bas Kleijn, The Frequentist Theory of Bayesian Statistics [2]

It appears that two accomplished frequentists have different opinions on bayesian statistics!

In general, the range of opinions about pretty much anything in statistics by the top people is … surprising? Confusing? Crazy?

No wonder that imposter syndrome is so widespread in data science.

Whatever your problem-solving approach is, you pretty much have a guarantee that somebody who is 10x smarter + accomplished published something somewhere that shows why the approach you used may be flawed.

References

[1] Wasserman, L. (2004). All of Statistics: A Concise Course in Statistical Inference. Springer Science & Business Media. https://lnkd.in/e-HMEz6Z

[2] Kleijn, B. (2022). The Frequentist Theory of Bayesian Statistics. https://lnkd.in/eMjpgtT5

item.title: Why Advanced Techniques to Reduce Runtime Often Do Not Work
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
A/B Testing: Why Advanced Techniques to Reduce Runtime and Sample Size Often DO NOT Work as Expected!

A key challenge in A/B testing is that the impact of new ideas is often very small. This typically requires large sample sizes and potentially long run times.

One potential solution: use sophisticated estimators and inference procedures to save on sample size and runtime. This can work well — but, unfortunately, not as often as we might hope.

Why? Let’s explore a specific example. Suppose you want to test your current setup, A, against a new idea, B. Assume that B is only slightly better than A on the primary metric. Further, imagine that with a sample size N and runtime T, your A/B test achieves only 40% power to detect a difference using Welch’s two-sample t-test.

Now, let’s say switching to a more advanced technique — like regression adjustment (possibly enhanced with machine learning) — increases power to 60%, using the same sample size N and runtime T. This sounds promising: 60% power compared to 40% is a meaningful improvement!

But here’s the problem. First, 60% power is still not great. Second, the goal was reducing runtime. If you do that, you reduce N and T and lower power. If N and T are decreased too aggressively, power could even drop below the original 40%! The result may come faster, but it’s still likely just another ‘not significant’.

Now, consider another scenario. Suppose the effect size is large enough that Welch’s two-sample t-test has 80% power with the original N and T. Suppose the advanced method boosts power to 95%. Here, reducing N and T might still leave you with around 80% power (which is sufficient), and the test completes faster.

In both cases, the advanced method improves power and is useful. Unfortunately, effects are often so small in practice that even real power improvements do not change much.

I remember leading a small research project to implement regression-adjusted estimators to improve A/B testing for email marketing. The goal was to test better on hard KPIs like revenue per customer or profit per customer. These KPIs have notoriously high variance, so even massive sample sizes only result in low power. We tested sophisticated methods, including ML-boosted regression adjustment [1], and literally used all available data from the database.

After many weeks of fine-tuning, we realized: we can get real power gains and transform mediocre test setups into good test setups. But some untestable setups will forever remain untestable setups.

Expectation management is key: data science is still just science, and not science fiction.

item.title: Why Warren Buffett’s Investment Philosophy is Helpful in A/B Testing
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
Why Warren Buffett’s investment philosophy is helpful in A/B testing too!

When we invest in stocks, we want to make money. Naturally, we try to focus on picking the “right” stocks that increase (hopefully soon). In A/B testing, we often think similarly, gain-oriented: we come up with some ideas about how a change can improve the business.

The problem? Just as stocks can not only go up but also down, A/B test ideas that should improve the business can actually hurt it.

Focus on gains is important, but focusing on limiting losses should not be neglected:

“The first rule of an investment is don’t lose [money]. And the second rule of an investment is don’t forget the first rule. And that’s all the rules there are.” — Warren Buffett

Why does Warren Buffett, one of the most successful investors of all time, say that? Here is some math. Suppose you invest 50k USD in some stocks. Suppose they lose 50% of their value, you panic, sell them, and end up with 25k. If you want to get back to the original 50k by investing in stocks again, you now have to double your investment. This is really hard … and even if you make it, you are basically just where you started!

This is why limiting risks is important.

Now, many people are frustrated with their A/B testing because they don’t get enough “significant” results. This often results in aggressive “searching for significance”: lowering the significance level, selectively removing outliers, running the test “until it reaches significance,” selectively searching for subgroups where “the result is significant”, and so on.

What is the consequence? Consider a simple A/B test scenario, where variant A is the baseline and variant B implements our idea. Suppose we strongly wish that B > A. If this wish is indeed true, the described aggressive significance searching can actually help to make the right decision! But if our wish is wrong, it can increase the chance of incorrectly concluding that our idea B improves the business (B > A), even though its implementation hurts the business (since A > B).

Even if we now find good ideas C, D, E, etc., we first still need to pay for the losses of our incorrect previous test result … just to get to the point where we started!

This is especially relevant if you try to improve something with A/B testing that already works close to optimum. For example, consider optimizing email marketing in a mature company. Suppose that the email marketing is already close to optimum with respect to revenue (or profit) per subscriber, and the goal is to further improve it by testing new ideas. Only a few ideas might improve the business, but many more can hurt it. Here, A/B testing can rarely deliver wins, because they are rare.

The key value here is limiting the implementation of ideas that make the business worse.

item.title: All A/B Test Sample Size Calculations Are Wrong, But Some Are Useful
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
A/B testing: most sample size and power calculations are wrong, but they can still be useful!

“My A/B test has 80% power at alpha = 5%”

Probably not!

Suppose we have a two-group A/B test and want to analyze it with Welch’s two-sample t-test, using H0: no effect. Assume, for simplicity, that using Welch’s test, based on a large-sample argument, is justified.

In this particular case, the true power depends on things we don’t know — for example, the true treatment effect and the unknown group variances. The true power is therefore also unknown.

When we perform a power analysis, we derive power for potential scenarios: what would the power be like if our assumptions for inputs like the true treatment effect and unknown group variances were true?

Sentences like “my A/B test has 80% power at alpha = 5%” are therefore misleading. For example, you might think you have 80% power, but if the true (unknown) treatment effect is much smaller than your guess, you could actually have just 58%, or 45%, or something else.

For the described setup, a better sentence would be: “There would be 80% power at alpha = 5% if I had sample sizes and , a treatment effect , and group variances and .”

Because there are multiple unknown parameters, it’s difficult to know how much power your A/B test will actually have. Any single power guess is likely wrong. (The key question is how wrong.)

However, a power analysis and sample size calculation are still useful. People often create a range for each input parameter and see how it affects power (e.g., “power curves”). This is often informative enough to make an educated guess about which effect ranges lead to low, medium and high power.

[1] is a great paper on the topic. A little spoiler from the first section:

“Broadly put, the power of a test is a function of three factors: the significance criterion (…), the sample size (…), and (…) population effect size (…). These four variables — power, significance criterion, sample size, and population effect size — are related such that when the values of three of these are fixed, the fourth is determined (…). A question that naturally arises is: Given that one doesn’t know what the population effect size is, how can power be computed? The answer is that power is computed for a given potential population effect size — and indeed can be computed for several different potential population effect sizes. (…) Thus it can be misleading to speak of the power of a given statistical test, because any particular test (…) actually has many different power values.”

Link to the article in the comment section.

Technical appendix

For a Welch two-sample t-test, the power equation contains seven parameters: the power , the sample sizes and , the variances and , and the means and . To solve for one we need the other six. For a 50/50 split where , we need to specify , , , and to obtain a certain power.

What are , , , and ? If we analyze the experiment based on data collected at the end of the experiment, they are unobserved true fixed population parameters.

The problem is twofold:

  1. Before the experiment: if these parameters were known, we would already have what we want and would not run the A/B test at all.
  2. After the experiment: we can only plug in estimates , , , and . For high-variance metrics like profit or revenue, these estimates often have high sampling variance and can be far from the true values.

In practice, , , , and are usually taken from previous time periods. Two sources of error arise:

  • The estimators from the historical period may be biased for the experimental period parameters.
  • Even if they are unbiased, the point estimates can still be far from the true values due to sampling variance.

Because point estimates will almost always differ from the true parameters, and the true parameters are unknown, sample size calculations will be wrong. They are still useful: a sample size calculation based on reasonable estimates puts you in the right ballpark, and the alternative — running experiments with no sample size planning at all — is worse.

item.title: Out-of-Sample Predictions Are Overhyped for MMM
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
Out-of-sample predictions are not only overhyped for Marketing mix modeling (MMM), but can actually be dangerous. Here is why.

Selecting and validating a MMM is the one of the toughest part in a MMM project. Model selection & validation using out-of-sample prediction is sometimes presented as a more “objective” approach to build an MMM.

The problem: Well-predictive models, based on out-of-sample predictions, can deliver substantially worse estimates than less-predictive models. (The keyword is “can” — not necessarily always.)

This is demonstrated in a paper by Peter Ebbes, Dominik Papies and Harald J. van Heerde [1]. They consider a linear model Y=Xb+e as data generating process (DGP), where analysts do not have access to some of the X’s. (A common situation in MMM, because variables that encode competitor marketing are typically unobserved.)

If you then use OLS to estimate the b’s you have model misspecification, in this case due to the omitted variable bias, which results in endogeneity. The result is that the OLS estimates are biased and inconsistent — so systematically incorrect.

If valid instrumental variables (IVs) Z are available, you can do IV regression and can get your b’s systematically right.

The problem? The authors in [1] remind us that using IV regression (which delivers good estimates of b) systematically delivers worse out-of-sample predictions than OLS (which delivers bad estimates of b) in this setup. Using out-of-sample predictions as selection criterion would conclude OLS > IV in this case. And confidently pick the bad estimates.

That said, out-of-sample prediction are important! Good MMMs typically should have a good out-of-sample prediction. But good out-of-sample prediction does not guarantee a good MMM and does not necessarily guarantee “objectivity” by removing bias caused by manual modeling.

This is why it is recommended to include geotests and lift studies in the model selection & verification process [2]. They can already deliver trustworthy estimates for some of the b’s you want to estimate. But — this is also not always the solution for all problems. The unobserved variables still trouble the estimation of the b’s. But now at least some trustworthy ground truth estimates are available for model selection and evaluation.

References

[1] Ebbes, P., Papies, D., & van Heerde, H. J. (2011). The Sense and Non-Sense of Holdout Sample Validation in the Presence of Endogeneity. Marketing Science, 30(6), 1115-1122.

[2] A New Gold Standard for Digital Ad Measurement: https://hbr.org/2023/03/a-new-gold-standard-for-digital-ad-measurement

item.title: Why Geotesting Always-On Media Can Produce Biased Estimates, Even in Perfect Setups
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
Marketing measurement: Geotesting always-on media can underestimate the iROAS, even in perfect test setups. (Here’s why — and how to deal with it.)

Geotesting is a popular method to measure the impact of advertising on key metrics. The typical setup compares control regions running the baseline media mix to test regions where the media mix is changed.

When testing always-on media, you need to pause advertising in the test regions. Even in an otherwise perfect test-control setup, this creates a challenge: if the tested media has lagged effects, earlier advertising can still influence KPIs during the test.

This can cause bias: because of pre-test media activity, the KPI drop in the test region won’t necessarily be as large as it should be. That means the incremental ROAS (iROAS) can be underestimated. We often describe the iROAS for a spend X as the revenue that only occurred because of the ad spend X, divided by that spend. But with lagged effects, earlier spend Z also affects the test period’s revenue, even though we’re trying to isolate the impact of X.

Whether this bias really matters depends on multiple factors — for example, the test duration and the length and shape of the lagged effects. If you plan a four-week geotest and lagged effects last only one week, the bias might be small. But if the test runs two weeks and the lag is one week, the risk of distortion is much higher.

A common fix is to run longer tests and exclude the early days or weeks from the iROAS estimate. This helps reduce the influence of lagged effects. While longer tests are sometimes unpopular due to concerns about lost revenue, that downside is often overstated [1].

In the optimistic case, you can decide which time points to exclude based on monitoring daily relative effects. For instance, if the first few days show small effects like -1% or -2%, and later stabilize around -6%, it appears reasonable to drop the early period from analysis (see picture).

This approach is more challenging (or impossible) when the effect is generally small — so effect variations are hard to detect — or when lag lengths are long and the test period is short. An imperfect test-control relationship would complicate things.

Monte Carlo simulations can be helpful for making these decisions: generate artificial data that mimics your real data and test how your method — e.g., CausalImpact, where a selected number of first days are excluded — performs under different lag and effect assumptions. This indicates how robust, precise, and insightful your results could be.

Geotests can yield strong insights, but often they’re not easy to design or analyze. Treat every geotest like a research project.

Technical appendix

The incremental ROAS for ad spends is often explained in a simplified manner as revenue that is only generated by spends (i.e. would not have happened without them), divided by these ad spends.

More formally, denote the revenue for the test region during the experimental time we would get at paid search spending level as . The incremental revenue is . Dividing that by gives the incremental ROAS.

That simplified formulation is usually not accurate anymore with lagged effects, because the pre-experimental spends need to be in the equation too. Denote the revenue for the test region during the experimental time we would get at paid search spending level , and pre-experimental spend , as .

When we are talking about incrementality and contribution of ad spends we typically want to compare a spending level (i.e.  and ) versus no spending (i.e. ):

However, an off-test with lagged effects and pre-experimental spendings often delivers us something that is more like:

The difference between these two expressions is the bias from lagged effects. A detailed introduction to the topic is in [1] and the references therein.

item.title: Formulating Marketing Impacts Precisely Is More Challenging Than It Appears
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
Data Science: formulating marketing impacts precisely (in the mathematical sense) is more challenging than it appears!

The causal impact of advertising, pricing, or other changes is typically described by comparing counterfactual scenarios. For example, to calculate the incremental ROAS for a channel, one first needs to derive how many sales would occur with a certain spending level and without it.

Many econometric papers focus on “average” effects and consider binary treatments. For example, many synthetic control papers consider cases with two potential outcomes — one with the intervention and one without.

This approach is intuitive and a great start, but it is not always flexible enough to accurately formulate marketing effects.

For example, a 30-day geotest to estimate paid search effectiveness — using selected sets of test and control regions — does not present only two scenarios. The reason is that budgets can be set every day, which leads to many possible combinations. Control regions might have zero spending for all 30 days, which can be represented by a vector of 30 zeros: (0, …, 0). Test regions might receive 10k on the first day, 15k on the second, and so on, which might be represented by another vector: (10k, 15k, …).

These vectors are sometimes called treatment histories [1].

A 30-day geotest can have many different treatment histories:

“It is clear from the definition that there are, in fact, many different (treatment effects): one for each pair of treatment histories. As the length of time of study grows, so does the number of possible comparisons.” [1]

On top of that we also have to consider lagged effects: if we spend today, we are likely to see effects in the following days.

Knowing how to formulate such effects precisely can be important in some cases. For example, consider geotesting for paid search again. Typically, companies have their paid search always on. In this scenario, a geotest requires shutting down advertising in selected test regions for a period of time. In the control regions, the standard advertising mix is maintained for comparison.

If paid search has lagged effects, activities before the experiment in the test regions can still influence KPIs during the experiment. Then the geotest does not necessarily test what we want — namely, comparing “some advertising” (control units) to “no advertising” (test units). Instead, the pre-experimental activities become mixed with the experiment.

One potential solution is to omit the first few days of the geotest — when lagged effects are expected — from the effect estimation. But decisions like this can be debatable. Knowing how to formulate treatment effects is a good basis for such decisions.

The first two sections in [1] are a great introduction on treatment effects in the dynamic scenario. There’s also a great Google paper [2], in particular section 4, that uses these ideas to formulate the ROAS. (That’s where the screenshot comes from.)

References

[1] How to Make Causal Inferences with Time-Series Cross-Sectional Data under Selection on Observables. https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/apsrev/v112y2018i04p1067-1082_00.html

[2] Bayesian Methods for Media Mix Modeling with Carryover and Shape Effects. https://research.google/pubs/bayesian-methods-for-media-mix-modeling-with-carryover-and-shape-effects/

item.title: Don’t worry about losing money with geotesting — it’s an investment
item.description:
Marketing measurement: don’t worry about losing money with geotesting — it’s an investment!

The idea behind a geotest: change the media mix in selected test regions, keep it steady in comparable control regions, and use statistical techniques to estimate the ROAS for the ad spend in question.

Launching or relaunching channels or campaigns with geotesting means increasing spend in test regions (“on-test”) while holding out spend in control regions. Geotesting campaigns or channels already live requires temporarily shutting them down (“off-test”). In both cases, some regions will see reduced advertising.

These potentially lost opportunities often worry marketers and leadership. Running the numbers usually tells a different story.

Cutting advertising only impacts revenue meaningfully if ROAS is strong. That’s often not the case. As John Wanamaker famously said: “Half of my advertising is wasted; the trouble is, I don’t know which half.”

If the actual ROAS is below target, the geotest helps cut losses while it runs and the insights can reduce future losses from inefficient spend.

But now let’s assume your advertising has a strong ROAS. Even then, sales are not entirely lost, because the saved budget can be reinvested later.

Here’s a simple example. A company spends $100K per month ($1.2M per year) on Google Ads. Assume the true ROAS is 2, which means $200K in incremental revenue per month, or $2.4M per year.

In April, the company runs a geotest and pauses Google Ads in half the market. It spends $50K instead of $100K, saving the rest. With a ROAS of 2, this leads to a $100K revenue drop in April.

At first glance, it seems like Google will now drive only $2.3M in revenue for the year instead of $2.4M. But that ignores the $50K saved, which can be used elsewhere.

In a pessimistic case, if the saved budget is reinvested at a ROAS of 1, the total contribution becomes $2.35M instead of $2.4M. The geotest “costs” $50K in lost revenue.

If the budget is reinvested at a ROAS of 2, total revenue stays $2.4M. Nothing was lost — it was just spent differently.

If the reinvested budget performs even better, say, at a ROAS above 2, the geotest increases total revenue, even though advertising was temporarily reduced!

How do you calculate the upside or downside of a geotest? You need to model different scenarios, because the true ROAS is unknown (after all, we run a geotest to estimate it). Start by creating a baseline with your planned spend and expected ROAS. Then build alternative scenarios that reflect temporary budget shifts and assume multiple ROAS levels.

The example below shows one potential scenario where the $50K savings are distributed as additional spend ($10K/month) in the 5 months after. (Edit: this is a simple example — in the real world, you’re dealing with multiple channels, each with its own spend and ROAS that change over time.)

Well-designed (!) geotests are usually a smart investment with a good risk-reward profile.

item.title: Should we really call A/B testing the ‘gold standard for causal inference’?
item.description:
Should we really call A/B testing the “gold standard for causal inference” in marketing and tech?

(Or perhaps a better question: when and how often?)

We often think A/B testing > quasi-experimentation > full modeling. But then we introduce a lot of additional assumptions in our A/B tests, bringing them closer to full modeling than we might want to admit.

Here’s an example. Suppose we are interested in the impact of something on metric Y, but we can only conduct an A/B test on a proxy metric Z (e.g., to gain more statistical power). Suppose we are interested in the long-term impact (e.g., 6 months) but only run the experiment for 1 month.

Can we still call A/B testing the “gold standard” in these cases? I would say no.

Essentially, we are interested in the long-term impact on Y, but we only get short-term results on Z. This is a slippery slope: we must combine evidence from the test with additional untestable assumptions to infer from short-term Z (what we measure) to long-term Y (what we actually care about). This can work! But maybe it does not. Also: getting reliable short-term results on Z can already be challenging (e.g., interference, data quality, etc.).

Now, we need to do something and A/B tests may be better than the alternatives in many cases. But in my opinion, the label “gold standard” is attached too often to results that don’t deserve it.

Back to the original question: should we really call A/B testing the “gold standard for causal inference” in marketing and tech?

item.title: When the synthetic control method works (and when it doesn’t)
item.description:
“When I first saw the synthetic control method, I had a really hard time understanding when it would work and when it would not.”

— Kyle Butts

Experimentation with synthetic control-type methods is, in many cases, a good way to estimate the impact of elements of your marketing mix.

The idea is to select one or several units — for example, stores, regions, or markets — as test units. For these, you change one or a few elements in your marketing mix that you want to test — for example, campaigns or channels, prices, opening or closing stores, promotions, and so on. Then you try to find multiple “suitable controls” for these test units.

The idea is to use the control units to create “synthetic twins” for the test units. A simple example would be to represent sales in New York as a weighted mix of sales in San Francisco, New Jersey, and Los Angeles.

This sounds intuitive. But why would it be mathematically justified to use a combination of different control units to create a “synthetic twin”?

So-called linear factor models are often used as justification. Key metrics like sales in each unit are shaped by many factors simultaneously: past and current paid advertising across multiple channels, organic traffic from various sources, referrals and word-of-mouth from customers, pricing and discounts, competitor actions, seasonality, economic conditions, and likely many more. Some of these factors are difficult or impossible to measure. But as long as the factors affect the units in a certain way, this is NOT necessarily a problem.

This post (where the original quote is coming from) explains these factor models: https://lnkd.in/et7JYa8Y

In the past few years, the synthetic control methodology has advanced significantly, and new approaches to justify its use have been developed. For example, check out this Spotify paper (https://lnkd.in/ed_n6x37) and the references therein.

See also: Synthetic Control Methods in Marketing: Theory and Practice — the full theoretical treatment in this repo, covering ASCM, BSC, GSCM, conformal inference, and Bayesian/frequentist comparisons.

item.title: Geotest before going national — commentary on Pranav Piyush’s YouTube example
item.description:
Pranav Piyush: “Most marketers launch YouTube nationally, but I told him there’s an easier (& cheaper) way: Running a geo-test.”

This is a great idea, if it can be implemented and you can measure your success metric on regional level.

Launch marketing in a few test regions and keep others as control (or exclude). If the marketing works great you can gradually add more regions (that’s advanced and not always possible) or go national.

The same can be done when budget needs to be cut: cut first in test regions and keep a few controls. Depending on the reaction and setup you can additionally cut in some control/exclude regions later. (That is advanced as well, and not always possible.)

Distribute your budget so that you learn while you earn!

item.title: The Overlooked Pitfall of Personalization with Causal ML
item.dc:creator: Oliver Brose
item.description:
[A/B Testing] One possible downside of personalization with causal machine learning.

Personalization with causal machine learning is a hot topic — and for good reason. It often allows companies to process vast amounts of data to deliver the right offer to the right customer at the right time. In many cases, this approach generates substantial business value.

But in some situations “granularity issues” can limit the overall impact.

Here’s an example to illustrate: imagine you’re using causal ML to decide whether or not to send a coupon to individual customers. This coupon could be displayed onsite, sent via direct mail, email, SMS or as a push notification.

Suppose management requires that the personalization logic ensures couponing stays at break-even profit within a four-month timeframe after the sending.

Now, let’s say you have 1 million customers annually eligible for personalized couponing. Suppose 10% of them have buying patterns that make sending a coupon profitable. For this 10%, suppose the average incremental profit per customer is $2.

The total added business value from causal ML-powered personalization would be: 10% × 1,000,000 customers × $2/customer = $200,000.

While $200k is something, it’s not a game-changer — especially for a large-scale initiative. When you account for technology, implementation, and labor costs, the initiative might even lose money. This happens despite having access to 1 million customers annually!

While this is a conservative example, similar scenarios are possible. To estimate the potential business value of personalization with causal ML, ask yourself:

  • How many people (N) are eligible?
  • What percentage (X) of them needs to drive improvement in key metrics?
  • How large does the impact (Y) per person need to be?

The higher N, X, and Y, the better.

For example, if 50% of users, instead of 10%, had an average incremental profit of $2 per customer, the situation would be completely different: 50% × 1,000,000 customers × $2/customer = $1,000,000.

Personalization with causal ML holds great potential, but it’s essential to do this math.

item.title: You think you run A/B tests, but often you actually run factorial experiments!
item.description:
You think you run A/B tests, but often you actually run factorial experiments!

To get more insights faster, different teams in the same company often run independent A/B tests (= 2-group randomized experiments) simultaneously. What are the consequences?

For a precise discussion, consider first a simplified setup: suppose 2 teams independently run 2 A/B tests, each with equal split, each on the same N people at the same time. Team 1 creates the first test with variants A1 and B1 and runs the test. Team 2 creates another test with variants A2 and B2 and runs it. What happens?

The random assignment of the two tests create these 4 variants:

  • group 1: A1 & A2
  • group 2: A1 & B2
  • group 3: B1 & B2
  • group 4: B1 & A2

For example, somebody is assigned to A1 (or B1) by the random assignment of test 1, and additionally assigned to A2 (or B2) for test 2. Each of the 4 groups gets approximately ~25% of the sample size N in our setup.

When team 1 analyzes its A/B test, it usually calculates the difference between the variant means, . This is the same as comparing groups 3 & 4 with groups 1 & 2:

The reason is that people in groups 3 & 4 have the assignment for variant B1, and people in groups 1 & 2 have the assignment for variant A1.

Team 1 may think it analyzes a 2-group experiment. But technically this setup is a 2×2 full factorial experiment with 4 groups, and calculating is close to what would be called “main effect” in the design of experiments (DOE) literature [1]. The same principle applies to the test of team 2: .

This principle scales if we increase the number of independent A/B tests on the same population at the same time, as mentioned in section 4.2 in a paper [2] by Ron Kohavi:

“If we set up each factor to run as a one-factor experiment and run all these tests concurrently we (…) get a full factorial in the end.”

(I think this paper is great and I recommend to read it!)

Now, in practice we often do not run the different A/B tests at exactly the same time and on exactly the same population. Some tests have different start and end points, possibly different populations, too. But in many cases the “factorial nature” remains: people are used multiple times for effect estimates across many A/B tests.

This is not a problem, by the way! The goal of this post is just to show the connection between overlapping A/B tests and factorial experiments — sometimes it is exactly the same.

Running factorial experiments should be done for the same reason as running multiple experiments simultaneously: you can get more & faster results.

If you want to learn more about factorial experiments check out my post [3] and the mentioned references therein.

item.title: Bayesian inference: are parameters fixed or random?
item.description:
“I was trying to re-learn Bayesian statistics (…) but it wasn’t clear (to me) what the data generation process in the Bayesian Framework actually is.”

— CrossValidated

In frequentist statistics it generally is assumed that there is a single true statistical model, often also called ‘data generating process’ (DGP). Usually the goal of a statistical analysis is to estimate some aspect of this DGP. For example, for a linear model we are often interested in the parameters .

In the frequentist world, parameters like the are considered fixed and unknown. In my opinion, that is emphasized a lot in textbooks.

In bayesian statistics we would specify priors for parameters like the . My impression: in the bayesian world people talk about the priors a lot (obviously!) — but other interesting aspects about parameters and the DGP sometimes receive less attention.

For example, are there true (fixed?) parameters? (What is the relationship to the prior?) What is the role of the prior in the DGP? Is there something as a single true DGP in bayesian statistics, as in frequentist statistics?

Here are two posts that I found useful to answer these questions.

First, Jonathan Bartlett wrote a blog post on the topic fixed vs. random parameters in bayesian statistics: https://lnkd.in/g9H425-r

Second, a great discussion about parameters and the DGP in bayesian statistics can be found on CrossValidated, where the quote from the beginning of this post is coming from: https://lnkd.in/gWNbEeXy

item.title: How to analyze factorial experiments when large samples are available
item.description:
A/B Testing: how to analyze factorial experiments when large samples are available.

Popular textbooks about the design of experiments (DoE) focus on domains where often only small samples are available for randomized experimentation. Examples are engineering, biomedical sciences or social sciences. Usually parametric methods are used for the analysis of these “small sample” experiments. The methods are typically specialized for certain setups, defined by

  • data type & distribution of the variable of interest (for example binary, normal or count data)
  • sample sizes per group (equal or unequal sample sizes per group, which can matter a lot in factorial experimentation)
  • group variances (homoscedastic variances vs. heteroscedastic ones)

Analyzing multigroup experiments with small sample sizes per group can require a lot of manual statistical modeling. This is because (a) many techniques are available for each setup, and (b) assumption checking like testing normality or for homoscedasticity is often required. It’s not easy!

But when large sample sizes are available — which we often have in marketing & tech! — it gets a lot easier. Then Wald-type tests work for numeric data types (i.e. continuous, binary and count data), regardless of unequal sample sizes per group and regardless of heteroscedasticity. Even without extensive assumption checking and statistical modeling!

These techniques are known, but don’t receive a lot attention in DoE textbooks. Where is good introductory material available? Check [1-4], links are in the comments.

item.title: What makes statistics and causal inference so difficult to understand?
item.description:
What makes statistics and causal inference so difficult to understand?

In my opinion the underlying logic: it’s about considering cases that could have happened, but didn’t, for summarised comparisons between reality and hypothetical scenarios that did not exist, but would have, if we had things done differently.

This way of thinking is simply not intuitive.

item.title: A/B Testing: What is the price of doing ‘freestyle statistics’?
item.description:
A/B Testing: what is the price of doing “freestyle statistics”?

It is best to analyze A/B tests with a pre-experimentally determined analysis plan. The reason is that doing steps like

  • an unplanned removal of data at the tails
  • an unplanned change of the success metric(s) after the original analysis
  • unplanned looping through an unspecified number of subgroups
  • …

… can, without proper consideration, easily have unintended consequences, for example “discovering” things that actually do not exist.

In the paper “Conditional As-If Analyses in Randomized Experiments” the authors look at another practice that appears to be pretty common in the experimentation world: analyzing a randomized experiment as if randomization scheme A was done, while actually randomization scheme B was done. What are the consequences of that? In the words of the authors:

“The injunction to ‘analyze the way you randomize’ is well-known to statisticians since Fisher advocated for randomization as the basis of inference. Yet even those convinced by the merits of randomization-based inference seldom follow this injunction to the letter. Bernoulli randomized experiments are often analyzed as completely randomized experiments, and completely randomized experiments are analyzed as if they had been stratified; more generally, it is not uncommon to analyze an experiment as if it had been randomized differently. This paper examines the theoretical foundation behind this practice within a randomization-based framework. Specifically, we ask when is it legitimate to analyze an experiment randomized according to one design as if it had been randomized according to some other design. We show that a sufficient condition for this type of analysis to be valid is that the design used for analysis be derived from the original design by an appropriate form of conditioning. We use our theory to justify certain existing methods, question others, and finally suggest new methodological insights such as conditioning on approximate covariate balance.”

Very interesting!

item.title: Nano influencers provide significantly higher ROI than macro influencers
item.description:
Insight:

“Our consistent result is that nano influencers provide a significantly higher ROI than macro influencers, namely by order of magnitude across empirical and field evidence.”

Data:

“We combine both empirical and field studies. On the one hand, we use a dataset from one of Europe’s leading DTC firms that includes 2,808 influencer-specific discount codes, allowing us to attribute 1,881,533 sold products (with total value over €17 M in revenue) to 2,808 unique sponsored postings on Instagram by 1,698 nano, micro, and macro influencers (three influencer followership levels, where nano refers to low-followership influencers and macro to high-followership influencers (e.g., Van den Bulte and Wuyts 2007)). On the other hand, collaborating with two DTC firms, we run three distinct field studies with a total of 319 paid nano and macro influencers (also on Instagram).”

Paper: Beichert, Maximilian, Andreas Bayerl, Jacob Goldenberg, and Andreas Lanz (2023), “Revenue Generation through Influencer Marketing,” Journal of Marketing, Forthcoming.

item.title: Identification of causal effects is an important topic in data science
item.description:
Identification of causal effects is an important topic in data science.

In many introductory causal inference courses and books the term “identification” is typically introduced as “how much can we learn about parameters from an infinite amount of data” [1, section 2.1]. That definition is probably sufficient for an introductory text.

But the topic of identification is much bigger and a little more complex:

“Over two dozen different terms for identification appear in the econometrics literature, including set identification, causal identification, local identification, generic identification, weak identification, identification at infinity, and many more.” [2]

“What does it mean to say that a quantity is identifiable from the data? Statisticians seem to agree on a definition in the context of parametric statistical models — roughly, a parameter is identifiable if the mapping is injective. This definition raises important questions: Are parameters the only quantities that can be identified? Is the concept of identification meaningful outside of parametric statistics? Does it even require the notion of a statistical model?” [3]

The paper “The Identification Zoo — Meanings of Identification in Econometrics” [2] is almost 100 pages! The paper “A General Theory of Identification” [3] tries to set general definitions to bring many of the existing versions of “identification” under one umbrella.

I would say [2] and [3] are good to read, but only for the truly interested crowd. The typical definition of identification from your intro to causal inference class should be enough for people who just use causal inference occasionally.

References

[1] Keele, L. (2015). The statistics of causal inference: A view from political methodology. Political Analysis, 23(3), 313–335.

[2] Lewbel, A. (2019). The identification zoo: Meanings of identification in econometrics. Journal of Economic Literature, 57(4), 835–903.

[3] Basse, G., & Bojinov, I. (2020). A general theory of identification. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.06041.
